subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 4-year-old boy is found to have an empty right scrotum on routine examination. The right testis is palpable in the inguinal canal. His parents are concerned about future fertility. Hormonal evaluation is performed.
question: Which of the following hormonal patterns is most consistent with unilateral cryptorchidism in this child?

options.text: Decreased inhibin B, increased FSH, increased LH, decreased testosterone
Increased inhibin B, decreased FSH, decreased LH, normal testosterone
Decreased inhibin B, increased FSH, increased LH, normal testosterone
Normal inhibin B, normal FSH, normal LH, decreased testosterone
Decreased inhibin B, decreased FSH, decreased LH, decreased testosterone

explanation_correct: Cryptorchidism is failure of one or both testes to descend. Impaired spermatogenesis from the higher intra-abdominal temperature lowers inhibin B, which removes negative feedback and raises FSH; LH rises as well. Because Leydig cells are largely temperature-resistant, testosterone is normal in unilateral cryptorchidism (it is decreased only in bilateral disease). These children also have an increased risk of germ cell tumors.

explanation_incorrect.A: This pattern with decreased testosterone fits bilateral cryptorchidism, not unilateral disease, in which Leydig cell function and testosterone are preserved.
explanation_incorrect.B: Inhibin B is decreased rather than increased, and FSH/LH rise rather than fall because of reduced negative feedback.
explanation_incorrect.D: Inhibin B is not normal, since impaired spermatogenesis lowers it, and testosterone is normal in unilateral disease.
explanation_incorrect.E: FSH and LH rise rather than fall in cryptorchidism due to reduced inhibin B negative feedback.

educationalObjective: Unilateral cryptorchidism shows decreased inhibin B, increased FSH, increased LH with normal testosterone; Leydig cells are temperature-resistant.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 15-month-old boy has persistent failure of the left testis to descend into the scrotum. His pediatrician discusses the natural history and management. The parents ask what should be done if the testis does not descend on its own.
question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate management and rationale in this child?

options.text: Immediate orchiectomy is required because the risk of germ cell tumor cannot be reduced
Hormonal therapy with exogenous testosterone is first-line to stimulate descent
Observation is futile because cryptorchidism never resolves spontaneously
Orchiopexy is only indicated if the testis produces no testosterone
Most cases resolve spontaneously; if not, orchiopexy should be performed before 2 years of age to preserve fertility

explanation_correct: Most cases of cryptorchidism resolve spontaneously. When the testis fails to descend, orchiopexy is recommended before 2 years of age to preserve spermatogenesis, since sperm develop best at temperatures below 37 degrees C. Cryptorchidism is also associated with an increased risk of germ cell tumors, and prematurity increases its risk. Orchiopexy lowers tumor risk and improves fertility outcomes.

explanation_incorrect.A: Orchiectomy is not the standard initial approach; the goal is to bring the testis down via orchiopexy to preserve fertility and allow surveillance.
explanation_incorrect.B: Exogenous testosterone is not first-line management for bringing down the testis; spontaneous resolution or orchiopexy is expected.
explanation_incorrect.C: Most cases do resolve spontaneously within the first months to years, so observation is appropriate initially.
explanation_incorrect.D: Testosterone production is often normal because Leydig cells are temperature-resistant; orchiopexy is indicated for fertility and tumor-risk reduction, not absent testosterone.

educationalObjective: Most cryptorchidism resolves spontaneously; persistent cases require orchiopexy before age 2 to preserve fertility and reduce germ cell tumor risk.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 15-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe right scrotal pain that began 2 hours ago while he was playing soccer. He has nausea and one episode of vomiting. On examination, the right testis is high-riding and exquisitely tender, and the cremasteric reflex is absent on the right. Lifting the testis does not relieve the pain.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Acute epididymitis
Incarcerated inguinal hernia
Ruptured varicocele
Testicular torsion
Hydrocele

explanation_correct: Testicular torsion is rotation of the testicle around the spermatic cord and vascular pedicle, classically in males 12 to 18 years old with a congenital bell clapper deformity (inadequate fixation). It causes acute severe pain, a high-riding testis, an absent cremasteric reflex, and a negative Prehn sign (no relief with elevation), often with nausea and vomiting. It is a surgical emergency.

explanation_incorrect.A: Epididymitis has a more gradual onset, localized posterior testicular pain, and a positive Prehn sign, not an absent cremasteric reflex.
explanation_incorrect.B: An incarcerated hernia presents with a groin mass and possible bowel obstruction signs, not a high-riding testis with absent cremasteric reflex.
explanation_incorrect.C: Varicocele is a chronic bag of worms swelling that does not cause acute severe ischemic pain.
explanation_incorrect.E: A hydrocele is a painless, transilluminating fluid collection, not an acute painful high-riding testis.

educationalObjective: Testicular torsion presents with acute severe pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex, and negative Prehn sign in adolescent males.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 16-year-old boy with acute onset right scrotal pain and a high-riding, tender testis is taken to the operating room with a suspected diagnosis of testicular torsion. Intraoperatively, the testis is found to be viable and is detorsed.
question: Which of the following best describes the correct intraoperative management?

options.text: Perform orchiopexy within 6 hours of symptom onset and fix the contralateral testis as well
Perform orchiectomy regardless of viability to prevent cancer
Perform orchiopexy only on the affected testis; the contralateral testis is never at risk
Delay surgery until Doppler ultrasound confirms absent blood flow, even beyond 6 hours
Manage with bed rest, ice, and oral antibiotics, as torsion usually resolves spontaneously

explanation_correct: Testicular torsion requires surgical correction (orchiopexy) within 6 hours to salvage the testis; manual detorsion is used if surgery cannot be done in time. Orchiopexy should be bilateral because the contralateral testis has the same congenital bell clapper fixation abnormality and is at risk for subsequent torsion. A nonviable testis is removed by orchiectomy.

explanation_incorrect.B: Orchiectomy is reserved for nonviable testes, not performed routinely when the testis is viable.
explanation_incorrect.C: The contralateral testis is at risk because the predisposing inadequate fixation is usually bilateral, so it should also be fixed.
explanation_incorrect.D: Doppler studies can support the diagnosis but should not delay surgery beyond the 6-hour viability window.
explanation_incorrect.E: Torsion does not resolve spontaneously and is a time-sensitive surgical emergency; conservative management risks losing the testis.

educationalObjective: Testicular torsion needs orchiopexy within 6 hours and bilateral fixation because the contralateral testis is also at risk.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 22-year-old man presents with a several-month history of a painless bag of worms swelling in his left scrotum that becomes more prominent when he stands and with Valsalva. It does not transilluminate. He and his wife have been trying to conceive for 2 years.
question: Which of the following best explains why varicoceles most commonly occur on the left side?

options.text: The left testis produces more sperm and thus generates higher venous pressure
The left gonadal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava at a sharp angle
The left pampiniform plexus has far fewer valves than the right
The right gonadal vein drains into the right renal vein at a 90-degree angle
The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at a 90-degree angle, creating higher resistance to flow

explanation_correct: A varicocele is dilation of the veins of the pampiniform plexus from increased venous pressure and is the most common cause of scrotal enlargement in adult males. It occurs most often on the left because the left gonadal (spermatic) vein drains into the left renal vein at a 90-degree angle, producing higher resistance to flow. Increased temperature can impair spermatogenesis and cause infertility. A right-sided varicocele suggests IVC obstruction (eg, from renal cell carcinoma).

explanation_incorrect.A: Sperm production does not determine venous pressure; the asymmetry is anatomical, related to venous drainage.
explanation_incorrect.B: The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, not directly into the IVC; it is the right gonadal vein that drains directly into the IVC.
explanation_incorrect.C: The left-sided predominance is explained by the 90-degree drainage angle into the renal vein, not a simple difference in valve number.
explanation_incorrect.D: The 90-degree angle of drainage into the renal vein applies to the left gonadal vein; the right gonadal vein drains directly into the IVC at a less acute angle.

educationalObjective: Left varicocele is most common because the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at 90 degrees, raising resistance; right-sided lesions suggest IVC obstruction.
source: Generated from 15. Reproductive.pdf - Pathology: Cryptorchidism, testicular torsion, varicocele

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 27-year-old man presents with a painless scrotal mass. On examination, there is a soft, irregular, worm-like swelling around the spermatic cord that enlarges with Valsalva and does not transilluminate. Ultrasound confirms dilated veins of the pampiniform plexus. He is compared with another patient who has a smooth, fluid-filled scrotal swelling that transilluminates brilliantly.
question: Which of the following statements about these scrotal lesions is correct?

options.text: The nontransilluminating bag of worms lesion is a hydrocele, while the transilluminating lesion is a varicocele
A spermatocele is a solid testicular tumor that never transilluminates
The varicocele does not transilluminate, whereas a hydrocele (serous fluid in the tunica vaginalis) does; a spermatocele is a paratesticular cyst from a dilated epididymal duct
Testicular tumors typically transilluminate because of their high fluid content
Both a hydrocele and a varicocele are benign lesions that readily transilluminate

explanation_correct: Varicoceles are dilated pampiniform plexus veins, palpable as a bag of worms, augmented by Valsalva, and they do not transilluminate. Benign scrotal lesions that do transilluminate include hydrocele (serous fluid within the tunica vaginalis; congenital from a patent processus vaginalis or acquired from infection, trauma, or tumor, and termed hematocele if bloody) and spermatocele (a paratesticular cyst from a dilated epididymal duct or rete testis). Solid testicular tumors do not transilluminate.

explanation_incorrect.A: This is reversed: the bag of worms lesion is a varicocele and does not transilluminate, while the fluid-filled transilluminating lesion is a hydrocele.
explanation_incorrect.B: A spermatocele is a benign cystic paratesticular nodule, not a solid tumor, and may transilluminate.
explanation_incorrect.D: Testicular tumors are solid masses and characteristically do not transilluminate.
explanation_incorrect.E: A hydrocele transilluminates, but a varicocele is a vascular swelling that does not.

educationalObjective: Varicoceles are nontransilluminating pampiniform plexus dilatations; hydroceles and spermatoceles are benign transilluminating fluid collections.
